payload.body: Asymmetry coefficient is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the asymmetry of the glottal airflow pulse within each glottal cycle: the ratio of the rising phase duration to the falling phase duration of the first derivative of the glottal flow waveform. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, the glottal cycle is partitioned into the rising phase (where g'(n) is positive, from minimum to maximum) and the falling phase (where g'(n) is negative, from maximum to minimum); the asymmetry coefficient is rising-phase duration / falling-phase duration. A coefficient near 1 indicates a symmetric pulse (typical modal phonation), while deviation from 1 indicates asymmetric closure — a longer falling phase (coefficient < 1) marks abrupt closure in pressed phonation, and a longer rising phase (coefficient > 1) indicates gradual closure in breathy phonation. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform g(n) — the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking which frames the cycle, (3) the first derivative of g(n) to locate phase boundaries. It is reported as a dimensionless ratio; maintained reference ranges separate typical from disordered phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed from the glottogram by voice-analysis software (Praat, laryngology suites), documented in the Dewaele glottal-source parameter set, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and maintained alongside the maximum-flow-derivative, the glottal-flow-declination-rate, the phase quotients, and the other glottal source parameters as a member of the voice-quality measurement map. e.g.: the asymmetry coefficient reported in a laryngology study comparing pressed and breathy phonation types; the asymmetry coefficient computed from a glottal-flow waveform in a laryngeal dysphonia case; the asymmetry coefficient value of 0.85 measured in a pressed-phonation assessment | not: glottal-flow-declination-rate (the steepest negative slope, not a ratio); maximum-flow-derivative (the peak positive slope, not a ratio) [formal: coeficiens inaequalitatis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: A human-made classification category made by laryngology and speech science to name the normal periodic mode of phonation so that breathy and creaky voice can be classified as deviations from it in clinical assessment and voice training.

definition.body: Modal phonation is the normal periodic mode of the phonation mode taxonomy: the mode in which the vocal folds vibrate with complete glottal closure each cycle, at a stable fundamental frequency within the speaker's modal range, producing periodic excitation of the vocal tract. It is the reference mode of the taxonomy: breathy and creaky phonation are defined against it, as deviations in closure and cycle character. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal configuration - medial adduction with complete closure each cycle (a high closure quotient) and firm contact, (2) the cycle signature - a stable f0 in the modal range with periodic, non-implosive cycles and no flow reversal, (3) the acoustic signature - a clean periodic tone with a strong harmonic series and minimal aperiodic noise. It persists as the reference mode of the phonation mode taxonomy: named in laryngology and phonetics, used in voice assessment (a breathy or creaky quality is classified as a deviation from modal) and in voice training (restoring or maintaining the modal mode), and maintained alongside the other modes in Sundberg's phonation inventory. e.g.: the modal-phonation mode in Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory; the 'modal voice' category on a voice therapy plan for a patient with habitual breathy voice; the 'modal voice' label in a phonetic description of a speaker's neutral sustained /a/ | not: breathy voice (incomplete closure with turbulent noise leak); creaky voice (low-f0 aperiodic implosive cycles); whisper (unvoiced glottal airflow) [formal: vox modalis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]
